prompt_version: s5-extract-facts-v2 (adapted from Paleo Atlas extract-facts-v3; v2 after Sofía's S5 review)

facts.statement: The study involved 102 adolescents, aged 10 to 17, of whom 55% were female, who took part in a fear learning test.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Participants were divided into two groups based on their recent exposure to fine air particles, using a standard limit of 9 micrograms per cubic meter.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Fear was measured by tracking sweat levels, watching for avoidance behaviors, and asking participants how scared they felt.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Those with higher exposure also showed a stronger return of fear when the threat was no longer present, indicated by higher sweat levels and continued feelings of fear.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Brain scans revealed that the high-exposure group had more activity in the right amygdala during learning and safety phases, and in the left insula during the recall phase.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Brain imaging was performed on a smaller group of 68 participants to look at specific areas of the brain involved in fear.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The findings suggest that higher air pollution exposure is linked to changes in how fear is processed, which may be a way air pollution contributes to anxiety.
facts.subject: humans
